cards.title: 87% of the Anthropic power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028

The Better Data Center Project says Anthropic has **no direct U.S. renewable commitments**; it estimates contracted U.S. sites will get **87% of their power from gas and 11% from coal** in 2028. cards.title: Perplexity and Intelligence

depth.text: OpenAI wants **perplexity** to track AI progress and help set shared **safety limits**

The post publishes OpenAI’s **internal pretraining measurements** and argues that lower **perplexity** tracks capability gains. Jakub Pachocki proposes shared industry norms and **development limits** tied to the metric, while noting that it misses chain-of-thought gains and can be hard to compare across labs.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters say perplexity is a clear, useful signal of broad AI progress; skeptics say it may mostly reflect the test data or task, not general intelligence.

cards.title: PostgreSQL Extensions in Go

depth.text: someone built a way to turn **plain Go** files into **PostgreSQL extensions**

Mark a function with //gopgext:function and it becomes a **SQL function**; the tool writes C glue, an install script and a control file. It also supports triggers, aggregates and index access methods, but the project calls it **experimental** and warns bugs can **crash the server or corrupt data**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some call more Postgres extensions a win for the ecosystem; others question Go's fit and say AI could write plpgsql instead.

comments.text: The Go community sold me on the necessity of programming mascots. The gopher is adorable, and I love seeing the creative tweaks for how people incorporate it into their marketing. From the same author: https://jespino.github.io/gokm/ (Linux kernel modules in Go)

More people using and extending Postgres is a huge win for the ecosystem, but I am somewhat uncertain of the appeal of Go for this task. It seems to really shine at "platform"-level tasks (e.g. K8s, network proxies, etc. etc.), while Postgres extensions are more at the data plane level.

cards.title: Fast-Anything: Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow

depth.text: someone built a tool to find **slow app code**, port it to **Rust**, and check it works
It records **real calls** and extra edge cases, then compares the port with the original; mismatches keep it off. It also rejects ports that are **slower per call**.

cards.camps: Two camps: proponents say selective Rust ports can help with hotspots; skeptics say bottlenecks are spread across the system or come from code choices, not the language.

comments.text: I would like to argue that one could make most codebases 50% faster if rewritten from scratch with performance in mind even in the same language. Taking python as an example, one could use benefit of hindsight and make better decisions from the start ( offloading slow parts to C binaries, better DS decisions, eliminating bloat etc.. ) if they rewrite the same app in Python. This is kind of what…

First of all, start with the measurements methodology, making sure that you're measuring a thing that actually matters for end users in all the various configurations on a setup that matches closely your production setup, otherwise results will never be completely conclusive unless you're trying to optimize a small piece and it gets flattened into noise on top of the overall picture. Significant…

neat, but in my experience bottlenecks that you could solve this way are low hanging fruits and optimized away quickly. the true performance hog is like sand, spread across the system, a little bit in every place.
It's also OK to rewrite in Rust because it's not just about performance. The fast part in other Python, Ruby, etc may be written in C/C++, or call an external library, and be the vulnerable part.

The reason rust is so tied to all the AI rewrites is because we see that the power of AI improves when the task has stronger verifiability. A stronger example is reverse-engineering: you have the final machine code to verify against. Performance of the final binary is still a bonus, but it's the strictness of Rust that makes it great for AI.

cards.title: PcapAnalyzer – self-hosted pcap analyzer with 27 problem detectors

cards.title: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as 'biggest breakthrough in decades'

depth.text: a **pancreatic cancer pill** helped tumours **shrink or disappear** in many people in a trial

The trial tested **daraxonrasib** in 61 people with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread; tumours stopped growing in **90%**. A year after treatment began, **76.6%** were alive; usually, 40-45% of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year. Doctors say it is not yet a cure.

cards.title: Jensen Huang's fall is bad news for Silicon Valley's accelerationists

depth.text: Jensen Huang's **fall** is bad news for Silicon Valley's **accelerationists**
Some commenters see his fall as part of a wider **political shift**; others say **AI will keep developing regardless**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some see Huang's fall as part of a wider political shift; others say AI will keep developing regardless.

comments.text: The gap in sentiment between most tech voices on X and mainstream media coverage of Jensen Huang is pretty incredible. The mainstream media coverage of the downfall of Jensen has been remarkably consistent and negative (almost gleeful), but you wouldn't know that if you read posts from any major VCs or tech figures.

Getting caught in the sights of things like violating sanctions or ITAR is an existential threat to your company. No matter how instrumental you think he is to the future success of Nvidia, there was immense pressure weighing on the board to remove him and he clearly understood this.

"The term accelerationism (specifically in the form of Accelerationists) first appeared in a book in Roger Zelazny’s 1967 science-fiction novel Lord of Light. The Accelerationists are a revolutionary faction (aligned with the protagonist, Sam) that advocates for the rapid, unrestricted deployment of advanced technology to shatter the ruling pantheon's stagnant monopoly and propel society…

I don't even know what a given CEO getting fired would have anything to do with "accelerationists". Huang or not AI is going to develop none the less... There's a lot of internet meta talk about AI that I think is completely disconnected from whatever will happen. You might be able to win some sort of meta war on the internet and maybe influence some politics, maybe, possibly, but actual tech…
Decel cycle ramping up after the mid-terms, that’s the bigger picture and Jensen is just a big cog in a much larger political wheel.

cards.title: Show HN: Zero C# – C# without a runtime or GC

depth.text: someone made C# build **native programs** with **no runtime or garbage collector**

It keeps **C#'s syntax, type checking and generics**, but memory comes from **arenas you free all at once**. The same source runs on Linux, macOS, Windows, WebAssembly and DOS on a 386; hello world is **11 KB on Windows and 40 KB on Linux**.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters see a niche for low-level C# without a runtime; critics say existing C# tools are enough and that porting code and managing memory aren't worth it.

comments.text: C# already provides many tools for your performance-critical code though. You can use pointers in unsafe. You can allocate unmanaged memory with Marshal. You can avoid copy with Span. You can even manually vectorise with Vector.IsHardwareAccelerated and such. You can also distribute apps without .NET runtime with NativeAOT. I'm sure there are people who want a C# without GC, but for me it's…

The GC is a feature. Not a bug to be eliminated. GC is not surrendering control. That seems to be HN's #1 bug bear. The sensation that someone or something is taking control away from you. The proper way to frame this is that you can actually focus on the original problem you set out to solve. Risking memory leaks is crazy when it's not something the customer is demanding. Even in gaming I think…

So... What does this have over using NativeAOT which already exists? Keep in mind a large portion of time NativeAOT is actually SLOWER than going through RyuJIT with the only definitive benefit being smaller binaries, and it's not like you can't do Span<T> and ref structs in modern C# for manual low level memory control already. So my question is just... why?

I looked for DLL support and found nothing. The standard library is also different from C#, and you have to manage memory on your own. Sadly I don't get the point. People code in C# for the .NET and its huge library, unless this is not a drop in replacement, you have to port your whole codebase; well then people will write Rust already...

Assuming this is very similar to bflat: it's a cool idea and fun to play with, but not very useful. C# is not designed to run without a GC, existing code usually won't run, because the standard library is missing. Just using C, Rust, Zig, or whatever is probably nearly always the better option. Those languages are designed to work without GC and provide various well established ways to manage…

cards.title: UK fridges secured from hackers

depth.text: UK fridges have been **secured from hackers**, but commenters say the **vulnerabilities** remain undisclosed

A commenter links a **Pen Test Partners press release** covering responses from the manufacturer, supermarkets and cold-store warehouse operators. It says researchers are **holding back the vulnerabilities** because they couldn't trace some device users.

cards.camps: One camp says fridges have no reason for an IP connection; another accepts internet-connected monitoring, but not internet-writeable temperature control.

comments.text: There's more information in the Pen Test Partners press release: * https://pentestpartners.com/security-blog/the-fridge-hack-uk... This includes who talked to whom and what the responses from the manufacturer, supermarkets, and cold store warehouse operators were. Don't expect to learn what the vulnerabilities themselves are, though. They couldn't get hold of and trace a subset of the device…

I'm surprised the fridges need to have far-remote control over their temperature in the first place. I can absolutely see the need for an internet-connected thermometer inside them to be able to alert when things go wrong off-hours, but that's a read-only resource. I can also understand the purpose of centralised temperature computer control through the local network, but that's not exposed to…

I'm quite curious to know what the actual attack was. The article is light on detail but does quote 'similar to weak password' but admits that it would have been necessary to get hold of an example device first, which isn't that hard as they're very common. To me this spells out an unprotected private key or secret residing in the device that could be used to break the authentication checks. In…

Stupid question: is there any reason these supermarket fridges should go up to above zero degree? If no maybe the user can set a hard limit that can only be manually overridden in store? At least it gives them more time before the food spoils?
Amazing, we hear so little about pro active work from govs, this is good.

cards.title: Two stealth models just appeared on the leaderboard, both ahead of Fable 5.2

depth.text: one **stealth design model** topped human designers and other AI models in a new test

The leaderboard from Contra Labs and BenchFlow uses blind votes on real client briefs: **Gestalt** has an Elo score of **1931** and a **90% win rate**. It ranks human designers second and Claude Fable 5.2 third; a commenter clarified that Gestalt is one model and the other bar is a human-created dataset.

cards.camps: Two camps: some question whether Gestalt exists or call the benchmark marketing; others are curious about its identity and what the result means.

comments.text: To clarify, it is not two models. Its a single model (Gestalt). The other bar on the benchmark is a human created dataset. Suffice to say we didn't expect anyone to beat it, but here we are. And no, it is not Contra model.

Thinky Chonky?

Glm 5.5 I bet, but still too early to tell

glossary.BYOP: Bring Your Own Power: when a data center arranges its own power generation instead of relying only on utilities.
glossary.marginal generators: Power plants expected to supply the extra electricity when new demand is added to the grid.
glossary.behind-the-meter: Power generated at a site and used there, rather than first going through the public grid.
glossary.PUE: Power Usage Effectiveness: a measure comparing all the electricity a data center uses with the electricity its computers use.
glossary.CO₂e: Carbon dioxide equivalent: a way to express the warming impact of different greenhouse gases as if they were carbon dioxide.
glossary.ZDR: Zero Data Retention: an arrangement where a service does not keep the information you send it.
glossary.inference provider: A service that runs an AI model and sends its replies to an app.
glossary.endpoint: A specific web address where a service can receive a request.
glossary.perplexity: A score for how surprised a language model is by text; lower scores mean it predicted the text better.
glossary.cross-entropy loss: A score for how far a model’s predictions are from the text it is meant to predict.
glossary.pretraining: Training a computer program on examples before using it for a particular job.
glossary.held-out dataset: Examples kept aside from training so people can check how well a model predicts.
glossary.chain-of-thought reasoning: A way for a model to work through a problem in steps before giving an answer.
glossary.reinforcement learning: A way to train an AI by rewarding choices that work and discouraging choices that do not.
glossary.immediate mode: A way to build a UI where the app describes what should appear each time it draws, rather than keeping a lasting set of controls.
glossary.retained mode: A way to build a user interface that keeps track of its parts between updates, so it can change only what needs changing.
glossary.system compositor: The part of a device’s software that combines visual layers into the picture shown on screen.
glossary.IME: Input Method Editor: a tool that lets someone type using a popup to choose characters or words.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.accessibility tree: A version of a webpage’s content that tools like screen readers use to explain it to people.
glossary.DSL: Domain-specific language: a small-purpose language made to describe one particular kind of thing, such as a user interface.
glossary.static recompilation: Translating a game's existing code into code for a different system before running it.
glossary.shader: A small program that tells a game how to draw an image or surface.
glossary.SPIR-V: A format for the graphics instructions produced by the project's shader recompiler.
glossary.Vulkan: A way for software to send graphics work to a graphics card.
glossary.subagent: A helper assigned a smaller part of a larger task.
glossary.terminal: A text window where you type commands to control a computer.
glossary.TinyGo: A tool that turns Go code into programs for more constrained environments.
glossary.C glue: C code that connects the Go code to PostgreSQL.
glossary.SQL function: Structured Query Language function: a named piece of code you can call from a database query.
glossary.aggregate: A database function that combines values from many rows into one result.
glossary.operator class: A set of rules that tells a database index how to search a particular kind of value.
glossary.foreign data wrapper: A PostgreSQL feature that lets it work with data stored outside the database.
glossary.goroutines: A way for a Go program to keep several tasks moving at once.
glossary.backend: The part of an app that does work behind the scenes, such as handling its data.
glossary.profiling: Measuring where a program spends its time so you know what to speed up.
glossary.hot function: A piece of code that takes up a lot of a program's running time.
glossary.Amdahl's law: A rule that speeding up one part of a program has limited effect if the rest still takes time.
glossary.protocol: A shared set of rules that lets different apps communicate.
glossary.interoperable: Able to work together, so people using different services can connect.
glossary.Fediverse: A collection of independently run social services that can communicate with one another.
glossary.instance: One separately run copy of a service, with its own operator and users.
glossary.ActivityPub: Shared rules that let different social networks exchange posts and account activity.
glossary.AT Protocol: A set of shared rules that lets separate social services work with the same network.
glossary.Matrix: An open set of rules for messaging that lets different apps talk to each other.
glossary.pcap: A file that records pieces of network traffic so you can look back at what happened.
glossary.DNS: Domain Name System: the internet's address book, which helps a computer find a website from its name.
glossary.retransmissions: When a device sends a piece of network traffic again because it may not have arrived the first time.
glossary.port scan: When someone checks many network connection points to see which ones respond.
glossary.API key: A secret code that lets software use an online service as an approved user.
glossary.KRAS inhibitor: A drug that switches off certain cancer changes that help tumours grow.
glossary.metastatic cancer: Cancer that has spread from where it began to other parts of the body.
glossary.remission: A period when cancer is no longer showing up, though that does not always mean it is cured.
glossary.CT scan: Computed tomography scan: a set of pictures doctors use to look inside the body.
glossary.clinical trial: A study that tests a treatment in people to see whether it works and is safe.
glossary.quantization: A way to make a model use less computing power by representing its internal numbers less precisely.
glossary.KL: Kullback–Leibler divergence: a score for how different one model's predicted answers are from another's.
glossary.GSM8K: A set of math word problems used to check how often a model gets answers right.
glossary.HumanEval: A set of coding tasks used to check whether a model can write working programs.
glossary.wiring harness: A bundle of wires that connects electrical parts around a car.
glossary.infotainment system: The car’s built-in setup for music and other screen-based features.
glossary.gut microbiome: The mix of tiny living things in your digestive system, which can affect how your gut works.
glossary.homunculus: A tiny imaginary person inside your head, used here as a picture of someone supposedly controlling your body.
glossary.NCIC: National Crime Information Center: a database law enforcement uses to share information on warrants and background checks.
glossary.read/write access: Permission to view information and change it.
glossary.benchmark: A test people use to compare how well different tools do a task.
glossary.spatio-temporal reasoning: Reasoning about where things are and how they change over time.
glossary.linguistic adversarial robustness: How well a model handles wording meant to trip it up.
glossary.human baseline: The human score used as a comparison point for model scores.
glossary.MCQ: Multiple-choice question: a question where you choose an answer from a list of options.
glossary.static website: A site made of pages meant to be sent as-is, rather than rebuilt for every visitor.
glossary.Cloudflare worker: A small program that Cloudflare runs to make or handle a webpage when someone asks for it.
glossary.JSON: A common format for storing and sending data in a way that programs can read.
glossary.cache invalidation: Deleting saved copies of pages so the next visit can get the updated ones.
glossary.CDN: Content Delivery Network: A network of servers that helps websites handle requests closer to their users.
glossary.CRUD: Create, Read, Update, Delete: basic actions an app can take on stored information.
glossary.R2: Cloudflare’s online file storage, where this site keeps its images and metadata.
glossary.server-side rendering: Putting a page together on the site's computer before sending it to your browser.
glossary.accelerationists: People who want advanced technology deployed quickly to push society forward.
glossary.DOS: Disk Operating System: basic computer software that lets other programs run and work with files.
glossary.TLS: Transport Layer Security: a way to scramble information as it travels between devices, so others can’t read it.
glossary.CGA: Color Graphics Adapter: an older PC graphics setup that could show a small range of colors.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.compiler: A tool that turns code you write into a program a computer can run.
glossary.macro lens: A lens made for taking very close-up pictures of small things.
glossary.magnification: How much bigger something looks in a picture than it does in real life.
glossary.Stulle: A German word for a sandwich.
glossary.runtime: The software that runs a program while it is being used.
glossary.garbage collector: A part of a program that finds memory it no longer needs so that space can be reused.
glossary.arena: A reserved chunk of memory for related things that a program can keep around or clear as a group.
glossary.generics: A way to make one piece of code work with different kinds of values.
glossary.NativeAOT: Native Ahead-of-Time: a .NET option that builds a program before it runs, so it can run without the usual .NET runtime.
glossary.WebAssembly: A way to run compiled programs inside a web browser.
glossary.386: An early kind of Intel processor that the DOS version is built to run on.
glossary.IP connection: A way for a device to send and receive information over a network.
glossary.private key: A secret digital key that can be used to prove an identity or act as its owner.
glossary.firmware: The built-in software that tells a device's hardware how to work.
glossary.Elo rating: A score that ranks competitors based on how they do against others.
glossary.blind head-to-head votes: People choose which of two designs works better without seeing which model made them.
glossary.AI slop patterns: Recurring signs that a design looks like low-quality AI output.
